claims.claim: In 1949 Levitt & Sons unveiled ranch houses at Levittown, New York, priced at $7,990.
claims.episode_span: began selling houses for $7,990 with no down payment for eligible buyers
claims.supporting_quote: these homes were only offered for sale, with a planned price of $7,990

claims.claim: Levittown houses were sold with no down payment under federal FHA housing supports.
claims.episode_span: selling houses for $7,990 with no down payment for eligible buyers. The houses came with VA-guaranteed loans and FHA mortgage insurance
claims.supporting_quote: the Levitt firm switched from rental to sale of their houses, offering ownership on a 30-year mortgage with no down payment and monthly costs the same as rental

claims.claim: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act (GI Bill) was signed in 1944 and provided returning WWII veterans with housing benefits.
claims.episode_span: the VA loan program authorized by the 1944 Servicemen’s Readjustment Act offered federal insurance and guarantees
claims.supporting_quote: Signed into law by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on June 22, 1944, this act, also known as the G.I. Bill, provided World War II veterans with funds for college education, unemployment insurance, and housing.

claims.claim: The Federal Housing Administration was created by the National Housing Act of 1934.
claims.episode_span: The FHA, created in 1934, and the VA loan program
claims.supporting_quote: is a United States government agency founded by President Franklin Delano Roosevelt , created in part by the National Housing Act of 1934

claims.claim: The US homeownership rate was 44 percent in 1940 and topped 60 percent within two decades after World War II.
claims.episode_span: the national homeownership rate rose from roughly 44 percent in 1940 to 62 percent by 1960
claims.source_title: Historical Census of Housing Tables: Homeownership (US Census Bureau)
claims.supporting_quote: the Great Depression drove the rate to its lowest level of the century--44 percent in 1940. The post-World War II surge in homeownership was remarkable. A booming economy, favorable tax laws, a rejuvenated home building industry, and easier financing saw homeownership explode nationally, topping 60 percent in just two decades

claims.claim: The FHA institutionalized redlining from 1934 until the 1960s, denying credit by neighborhood on racial grounds.
claims.episode_span: FHA and VA appraisal standards treated racial homogeneity as a marker of neighborhood stability, so loans rarely reached Black buyers
claims.supporting_quote: The federal government played a key role in institutionalizing and encouraging redlining through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). The FHA was the architect of federally sponsored redlining from 1934 until the 1960s.

claims.claim: The 1968 Fair Housing Act banned racially motivated redlining, and Congress passed the Community Reinvestment Act in 1977.
claims.episode_span: Fair-housing legislation in 1968 and the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 attempted to correct racial exclusion
claims.supporting_quote: In 1977, Congress passed the Community Reinvestment Act to affirm the obligation of federally regulated financial institutions, such as banks, to reinvest in the low- and moderate-income communities where they operate

claims.claim: The National Interstate and Defense Highways Act, authorizing the interstate highway system, became law on June 29, 1956.
claims.episode_span: the combination of cheap mortgage credit and federal highway construction after 1956 made distant greenfield sites economically attractive
claims.source_title: National Interstate and Defense Highways Act (1956) | National Archives
claims.supporting_quote: to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 to provide additional revenue from the taxes on motor fuel, tires and trucks and buses; and for other purposes; June 29, 1956

claims.claim: The mortgage interest deduction has existed since the federal income tax began in 1913.
claims.episode_span: The mortgage interest deduction, already on the books since the income-tax code of 1913
claims.supporting_quote: The deduction existed at the birth of the income tax in 1913—a tax explicitly designed to hit only the richest individuals, a group for whom homeownership rates were not a social concern.
